content.title: The World He Was Born Into: Jahiliyyah from Within
paragraphs: Chapter 3
The World He Was Born Into: Jahiliyyah from Within

After the death of his grandfather ‘Abd al-Muttalib, Muhammad, may Allah’s peace and blessings be upon him, grew up in the household of his uncle Abu Talib. Before following the events of his youth, it helps to understand the world around him. The word Jahiliyyah (the religious, social, and moral condition that prevailed before the Prophet’s mission) does not mean that the Arabs knew nothing or had no civilization.

The Arabs had a rich poetic tradition, carefully preserved genealogies, markets, long-distance trade, and customs that organized parts of social life. They also admired generosity, courage, loyalty, and protection of the neighbor. Yet alongside these strengths were beliefs and systems that had moved far from revealed guidance. The Qur’an therefore speaks of “the judgment of Jahiliyyah” when people replace Allah’s guidance with standards of their own.
Do they seek the judgment of the times of ignorance? Who could be better than Allah in judgment for people who are certain in faith?
Qur’an 5:50 — QuranEnc, Rowwad Translation Center

The central religious problem was shirk (directing an act of worship to someone or something besides Allah, or giving another a share in worship). Many Makkan polytheists acknowledged that Allah was the Creator, yet they did not worship Him alone. Idols stood around the Ka‘bah, and people called upon intermediaries whom they claimed would bring them nearer to Allah. Tawhid was therefore not simply the statement that Allah exists; it returned worship, supplication, sacrifice, vows, and reliance to Allah alone.

true devotion is due to God alone. [As for] those who choose other protectors beside Him, saying, ‘We only worship them because they bring us nearer to God,’ God Himself will judge between them regarding their differences. God does not guide any ungrateful liar.
Qur’an 39:3 — M. A. S. Abdel Haleem, published translation on Quran.com.

Idolatry also produced rules that entered ordinary life. Certain animals were dedicated to the idols and given names that can be confusing to a first-time reader: Bahirah (a she-camel whose milk was withheld and dedicated to the idols), Sa’ibah (an animal released for the idols and no longer ridden or used for carrying), Wasilah (a she-camel set aside for the idols after giving birth to female offspring in a particular sequence), and Ham (a breeding camel exempted from riding or carrying after producing a set number of offspring). These were not laws from the religion of Abraham, peace be upon him, but human customs treated as sacred legislation.

Allah did not ordain any such thing as the Bahīrah, Sā’ibah, Wasīlah, and Hām [i.e., dedicated camels to idols]. Rather those who disbelieve fabricate lies against Allah, and most of them do not understand.
Qur’an 5:103 — QuranEnc, Rowwad Translation Center

An authentic hadith mentions ‘Amr ibn Luhayy al-Khuza‘i, whose name became associated with changing parts of the religion inherited from Abraham, peace be upon him. The Prophet, may Allah’s peace and blessings be upon him, said that he was the first to institute the sa’ibah. In other words, he introduced the practice of setting certain animals apart for idols so that they were no longer used normally. A custom repeated for generations can eventually look like religion itself.

The Prophet said: “I saw `Amr bin ‘Amir bin Luhai Al-Khuza`i dragging his intestines in the (Hell) Fire, for he was the first man who started the custom of releasing animals (for the sake of false gods).”
Sahih al-Bukhari 3521 — published English translation on Sunnah.com

People also sought guidance through a kahin (a soothsayer who claimed knowledge of hidden matters and could be consulted in disputes or decisions), through azlam (special arrows used to decide whether to do or avoid something), and through omens (treating a bird, sign, or event as a reason to proceed or turn back). These practices could affect travel, marriage, and disputes, so the Qur’an explicitly condemned seeking decisions through divining arrows.
Also it is forbidden to use arrows [of chance] to determine your decisions. This is all evil practice.
Qur’an 5:3 (excerpt) — QuranEnc, Rowwad Translation Center

Even the Hajj connected to the House built by Abraham and Ishmael, peace be upon them, had acquired changes. Quraysh and those who followed their special pilgrimage customs were called al-Hums (Quraysh and groups that followed their strict pilgrimage practice because they considered themselves the people of the Sacred Precinct). The Haram is the sacred area surrounding Makkah. ‘Arafah, where pilgrims stand on the Day of ‘Arafah, lies outside the Haram, while Muzdalifah lies inside it, between ‘Arafah and Mina. The Haram has defined boundaries. The departure mentioned here, known as ifadah, is the pilgrims’ movement from ‘Arafah towards Muzdalifah after completing their standing at ‘Arafah. Al-Hums said that, as people of the Haram, they should not leave it, so they stopped at Muzdalifah instead of standing at ‘Arafah with the other Arabs. Islam abolished that self-made privilege. ‘Aishah, may Allah be pleased with her, explained that Quraysh and their followers used to stand at Muzdalifah, whereas the rest of the Arabs stood at ‘Arafah; Islam ordered the Prophet to stand at ‘Arafah and then depart from there (Sahih al-Bukhari 4520; Sahih Muslim 1219).
Then move on from where the people move on, and seek Allah’s forgiveness, for Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.
Qur’an 2:199 — QuranEnc, Rowwad Translation Center

Another change concerned the clothes worn in tawaf (circling the Ka‘bah as an act of worship). An authentic report states that some Arabs would circumambulate naked unless al-Hums gave them clothes: a man would give a man clothing and a woman would give a woman clothing. If a visitor could not obtain these special clothes, some would perform tawaf naked. This was not simply forgetting modesty; a man-made religious rule had turned access to particular clothing into part of the ritual. Revelation restored covering and dignity to worship.

‘Urwah ibn al-Zubayr reported that Arabs outside al-Hums would circumambulate the Ka‘bah unclothed unless al-Hums provided them with garments. Men of al-Hums supplied clothing to men, and women supplied clothing to women.
Report of ‘Urwah ibn al-Zubayr in Sahih Muslim 1219b.
O children of Adam, take your adornment [i.e., wear your clothing] at every masjid, and eat and drink, but be not excessive. Indeed, He likes not those who commit excess.
Qur’an 7:31 — Saheeh International, published translation on Quran.com.

Marriage as we recognize it also existed: a man sought a woman from her guardian, gave her a marriage gift, and married her. But ‘Aishah, may Allah be pleased with her, reported that other forms also existed before Islam. She summarized four types: the familiar marriage; a form in which a husband asked his wife to conceive by another man; a form in which fewer than ten men had relations with one woman and she later assigned the child to one of them; and a form in which many men visited a woman and the child was later attributed by resemblance. Islam abolished these forms and retained the recognized marriage (Sahih al-Bukhari 5127), protecting lineage and family rights.

Among the harshest practices found in some tribes and circumstances was female infanticide (killing a baby girl by burying her alive). It is wrong to imagine that every Arab family did this, but the practice existed and the Qur’an presents the murdered girl herself in the scene of Judgment, being asked for what crime she was killed. At the same time, people’s attitudes and conduct were not all alike: Asma bint Abi Bakr, may Allah be pleased with her, reported that Zayd ibn ‘Amr ibn Nufayl used to stop fathers from killing their daughters and would offer to support the girls himself (Sahih al-Bukhari 3828).
and when the baby girl buried alive is asked, for what crime she was killed,
Qur’an 81:8–9 — QuranEnc, Rowwad Translation Center

The tribe (a large network of families linked by ancestry and alliance) also had two sides. It could protect a person who would otherwise be vulnerable, because relatives and clan stood behind him. But this could become ‘asabiyyah (supporting one’s group simply because it is one’s group, even when it is wrong), producing long feuds and resistance to truth. The Prophet later warned that traces of Jahiliyyah could remain even among Muslims, including boasting of family status, insulting other lineages, attributing rain to the stars, and wailing over the dead with loud cries of anguish and resentment.

Among my people there are four characteristics belonging to the pre-Islamic period which they do not abandon: boasting of high rank, reviling other people’s genealogies, seeking rain by the stars, and wailing.
Sahih Muslim 934 — excerpt from the published English translation of Mishkat al-Masabih 1727 on Sunnah.com.

The marketplace also needed reform. Riba (including a stipulated increase on a loan or debt and prohibited forms of exchange) and tatfif (taking one’s own measure in full but giving others less when selling or weighing) were known. The Qur’an therefore did not separate religion from commercial honesty; it opened an entire surah with a warning to those who cheat in measure and weight.
Woe to the defrauders, those who take full measure when they take from others, but they give less when they measure or weigh for them.
Qur’an 83:1–3 — QuranEnc, Rowwad Translation Center

Yet Jahiliyyah should not be told as though every person and every custom were evil. The Arabs included people known for generosity, courage, loyalty, protection of guests, and helping the oppressed. Islam did not destroy every existing quality; it gave good qualities a sound standard. Generosity did not need to be abolished, but it needed faith and justice; courage was to be preserved without turning into oppression or blind tribal loyalty. The Prophet taught that those who were among the best people in Jahiliyyah could also be among the best in Islam when they gained true understanding.
You find people like metal; the best of them in the pre-Islamic era are the best of them in Islam, if they understand.
Sahih al-Bukhari 3493; Sahih Muslim 2526 — excerpt from the second narration in HadeethEnc 6367, published English translation.

The same principle applied to alliances. A hilf (an agreement between families or tribes to support one another or pursue a common purpose) could be based on unjust tribal solidarity, but it could also serve justice. Hilf al-Fudul was a famous Makkan agreement in which clans pledged to stand with an oppressed person until his right was restored. Muhammad, may Allah’s peace and blessings be upon him, witnessed it before prophethood, and its details will appear in the next chapter. Islam rejected alliances built on wrongdoing but strengthened commitments to justice.
There is no alliance in Islam, and Islam strengthened the alliance made during pre-Islamic days.
Sahih Muslim 2530; Sunan Abi Dawud 2925 — published English translation of the parallel narration in Sunan Abi Dawud on Sunnah.com.

Nor was everyone in Makkah satisfied with idolatry. Seerah sources preserve reports of the hunafa (individuals who rejected idol worship and searched for the religion of Abraham, peace be upon him) such as Zayd ibn ‘Amr ibn Nufayl, Waraqah ibn Nawfal, ‘Uthman ibn al-Huwayrith, and ‘Ubayd Allah ibn Jahsh. They did not form one organized religion and their paths did not all end in the same place. Zayd is a clear example: he rejected sacrifice to idols, searched for Abraham’s religion, and Asma bint Abi Bakr, may Allah be pleased with her, reported seeing him lean against the Ka‘bah and tell Quraysh that they had departed from Abraham’s religion (Sahih al-Bukhari 3828).

This was therefore a complex world: the Ka‘bah stood and was honored, yet idols surrounded it; Hajj was known, yet human rules had entered its rites; the tribe could protect the weak, yet blind loyalty could support injustice; trade brought wealth to Makkah, yet riba and cheating were present; and alongside genuine generosity and courage stood serious religious and social wrongs. Revelation would come to this real society and separate what was true from what was false: tawhid instead of shirk, justice instead of blind tribalism, dignity instead of corrupt customs, and fulfillment of rights instead of exploitation—while preserving truthfulness, generosity, loyalty, and every quality consistent with what is right.

Within this society Muhammad, may Allah’s peace and blessings be upon him, was growing up in Abu Talib’s home. He saw Makkah, its markets, tribes, pilgrimage, and customs before anyone knew him as a Prophet. The next stage brings us closer to his own life: his work, tending sheep, experience in trade, the events he witnessed in youth, and the reputation by which the people of Makkah knew him before they ever heard the first verse of revelation.
